name: PulsePoint AerWork Pulmonary Work Implant
body_location: thoracic — subpleural and diaphragmatic; bilateral bronchial wall nodes
description:
The AerWork is a pulmonary efficiency implant engineered for workers who require sustained high-output respiratory performance across long shifts — not elite athletes chasing peak performance, but the broader population of physical laborers, singers, divers, and industrial workers whose lungs are their primary professional tool. The implant comprises three integrated components: a set of 12 subpleural compliance nodes distributed across the visceral pleura of both lungs that modulate local tissue elasticity, allowing the lung parenchyma to expand more fully during inhalation and recoil more efficiently during exhalation, increasing functional residual capacity by 15–25% in most users; a pair of bronchial diameter regulators at the main stem bronchi that maintain optimal airway caliber during exertion, counteracting the bronchoconstriction that degrades performance during sustained physical work; and a diaphragmatic pacing module that interfaces with the phrenic nerve to optimize the timing and depth of diaphragmatic contraction, reducing the accessory muscle recruitment that leads to respiratory fatigue over long shifts. The system does not provide supplemental oxygen — it makes the lungs more efficient at using the air that is already available.

The AerWork was designed with GLMZ's working population in mind, particularly the large cohort of laborers in the city's lower tiers who work in environments with compromised air quality — construction sites with particulate, industrial processing floors, and the lower-level infrastructure zones where ventilation is substandard. By improving respiratory efficiency, the implant reduces the ventilatory drive that forces workers to breathe harder in these environments, which in turn reduces total particulate inhalation over a career. Commercial divers working the Lake Michigan utility infrastructure, singers performing in large venues without acoustic amplification, firefighters and emergency responders, and endurance delivery workers all use it. Workers who have the AerWork describe the sensation of physical labor as less breathless — the feeling of running out of air at the end of a hard push simply happens later and recovers faster. For singers, the improvement in breath support translates directly to longer phrases, more dynamic control, and less performance anxiety about sustaining difficult passages.
installation_requirements: Thoracic specialist clinic; general anesthesia required; bilateral bronchoscopic and subpleural installation; 2-week inpatient or monitored recovery; pulmonary function testing required pre- and post-installation
maintenance: Biannual pulmonary function testing and node integrity check at PulsePoint certified respiratory clinic; diaphragmatic pacing module is firmware-updated wirelessly; compliance nodes rated for 10-year service life

side_effects: Mild pleuritic chest discomfort during the 2-week recovery period as subpleural nodes integrate
Some users experience a brief period of heightened awareness of their own breathing — described as feeling 'too conscious' of respiratory rhythm — that resolves within 2–4 weeks
Rare cases of diaphragmatic pacing desynchronization during high-fever illness, causing irregular breathing rhythm that resolves when fever clears
A small percentage of users report vivid dreams involving breathing or submersion during the first calibration period of the pacing module
cultural_context: The AerWork sits at a slightly different social register than most PulsePoint consumer products because its Licensed status and surgical complexity push it out of the walk-in-clinic tier and into the domain of planned professional investment. In Tier 2 and 3 working communities, it is aspirational rather than ubiquitous — something people save toward or negotiate as part of an employment package. Among commercial divers and emergency services workers, it is close to standard-issue, and several corponations in the Lake Michigan industrial sector include it in senior technician contracts. In performing arts communities, the AerWork is openly discussed and professionally respected; vocal coaches and wind instrument teachers sometimes recommend it to students entering competitive conservatory programs. The Licensed requirement is a minor administrative friction rather than a real barrier — the licensing process involves a standard pulmonary function evaluation and takes one clinic visit.
known_users: Commercial divers working Lake Michigan utility and freight infrastructure
Construction workers and industrial laborers in low-ventilation environments
Professional singers and wind instrument performers
Endurance delivery workers and couriers on high-vertical routes
Competitive swimmers and underwater sports practitioners
story_hooks: A commercial diver with an AerWork implant is found drowned in a sealed section of the Lake Michigan utility tunnels — the coroner notes the drowning took far longer than it should have given the implant's capacity, suggesting the diver was conscious and trapped for an extended period before death, and the pacing module's logs may tell exactly what happened.

A series of AerWork units installed through a licensed clinic in the Shelf's industrial zone are logging anomalous bronchial dilation events that correlate precisely with a specific airborne chemical compound — someone is testing an aerosolized agent in the district, and the implants are the only evidence.

A conservatory student with an AerWork is accused of cheating in a breath-control competition — the institution's rules are ambiguous on pulmonary implants, and the resulting hearing is drawing attention from both performing arts advocacy groups and corponation lobbyists who have very different interests in the outcome.
